questions.stem: In the ED you are taking consent from Jenny, 32, for an urgent lumbar puncture for suspected meningitis. She has a GCS of 15, sharp optic discs and no focal signs. She asks what is most likely to go wrong afterwards. Which complication should you tell her is the most common?
options: Brain herniation (coning) causing drowsiness and trouble breathing
A headache that is worse sitting or standing and eases lying flat
Bleeding around the spinal nerves causing weakness in the legs
Infection at the needle site spreading into the spine
questions.why: Post-dural puncture headache is the most common complication of an LP. It is caused by CSF leaking through the dural hole, is typically postural (worse upright, better lying flat) and usually settles within days. Tell her about it first and say it can be treated.
notes: Herniation is a rare but serious risk and is very unlikely without signs of raised intracranial pressure, which Jenny does not have. Mention it, but not as the most likely problem.
A spinal haematoma is rare and is mainly a risk with anticoagulants or a bleeding disorder. Jenny has neither, and her clotting and platelets are normal.
Infection is a rare risk when aseptic technique is used and the skin is intact, as hers is. It is far less common than post-LP headache.

questions.stem: At 11:00 the laboratory phones Jenny's CSF Gram stain through: Gram-positive diplococci. Jenny, 32, had dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV at 10:45. She is immunocompetent, not pregnant, has no allergies and has normal renal function. What is the most appropriate change to her antimicrobial therapy now?
options: Change ceftriaxone to IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly
Add IV amoxicillin 2 g 4-hourly to cover Listeria monocytogenes
Add IV vancomycin (loading dose 25–30 mg/kg) until susceptibilities return
Add IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly to cover herpes simplex virus
questions.why: Gram-positive diplococci in CSF mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, which may be resistant to penicillin or ceftriaxone. eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone until susceptibilities are known, then narrowing treatment to fit the organism.
notes: Switching to benzylpenicillin is only right once the isolate is shown to be susceptible. Doing it before then risks failing to treat a resistant pneumococcus.
Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus. Empirical cover is only for people over 50, immunocompromised patients, pregnant women or people with alcohol dependence, and Jenny is none of these.
She has a bacterial CSF picture with organisms seen and no confusion, seizures or focal signs, so herpes simplex encephalitis cover is not indicated.

questions.stem: Jenny, 32, has pneumococcal meningitis. She received dexamethasone 10 mg IV straight after her LP, just before her first dose of ceftriaxone. A student asks why the steroid has to be given before or with the first antibiotic dose rather than later. What is the main mechanism behind its benefit?
options: It blunts the cytokine surge when antibiotics lyse bacteria and release cell wall products
It increases ceftriaxone penetration across the inflamed blood–brain barrier
It reduces CSF production by the choroid plexus, which stops intracranial pressure rising
It directly slows pneumococcal replication within the subarachnoid space
questions.why: When beta-lactams lyse bacteria, cell wall components and pneumolysin are released. These trigger TNF and IL-1 and subarachnoid inflammation, which damage the brain and cochlea. Dexamethasone given before or with the first dose damps this surge, reducing deaths and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis.
notes: Dexamethasone does the opposite: it makes the blood–brain barrier less leaky. This can reduce antibiotic penetration, especially of vancomycin.
Cutting CSF production is how acetazolamide works. It is not the reason dexamethasone helps in bacterial meningitis.
Corticosteroids have no antibacterial action. Their benefit comes from modifying the host's inflammatory response.

questions.stem: The ED registrar positions Jenny, 32, on her left side with her knees drawn to her chest for a lumbar puncture, aiming for the L3/4 interspace. Which surface landmark best guides her to the right level?
options: A line joining the posterior superior iliac spines (the sacral dimples)
A line joining the lower borders of the 12th ribs posteriorly
A line joining the inferior angles of the scapulae
A line joining the highest points of the iliac crests
questions.why: The supracristal (Tuffier's) line joining the tops of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4/5 interspace. The space just above it is L3/4. These levels are well below the conus medullaris, which ends at about L1/2 in adults, so the needle meets only nerve roots floating in CSF.
notes: The posterior superior iliac spines lie at about S2, the level where the dural sac ends. That is too low for a standard LP.
The 12th ribs are near the T12/L1 level, which is at or above the conus medullaris. Going in there would risk injuring the spinal cord.
The inferior angles of the scapulae lie at about T7. This is a thoracic landmark and has nothing to do with lumbar puncture.
